idiom_name: Readonly types plus Map or WeakMap registry behind a factory function; Symbol.for handles
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds the compile-time lock the JavaScript realization lacks: the flyweight is typed Readonly<T> (or declared with readonly properties), the pool is a Map<string, Readonly<T>> or a WeakMap for object keys, and the factory's return type is what callers see, so writing to shared state fails to compile. Immutable updates through spread or a persistent-collections library replace in-place writes, Object.freeze enforces the same rule at runtime, and Symbol.for provides process-wide canonical handles. The compiler cannot check the intrinsic/extrinsic split, so encode it in the type names and keep the read-only view as the only exported shape of the shared object.
pitfalls: Readonly<T> is shallow: nested objects and arrays stay assignable through the read-only view, so a flyweight containing a mutable array can still be changed by callers.
readonly is erased at compile time; plain JavaScript callers (or any cast) can still write to the object, so Object.freeze or private state is required for a real runtime guarantee.
A module-level Map is a process-wide strong reference and leaks with unbounded keys; use WeakMap when the key is an object, remembering that strings cannot be weak keys.
Template-literal keys allocate on every lookup and a key that omits part of the intrinsic state shares the wrong object - the two most common ways the factory silently misbehaves.
